readings.w: Irenaeus in Greek as Eusebius quotes him (Church History 3.36.12: hina katharos artos heurethō), and Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 16: ut panis mundus inveniar); Lake's footnote: 'om. Iren. gr., Hieron.'
readings.en: I may be found pure bread

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and his Greek and Latin witnesses. Lightfoot thinks it 'probable from a comparison of these authorities that the genitive should be omitted altogether', and brackets 'of Christ'.
b: Jerome's Latin reads Frumentum Christi sum, dentibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar: mundus is the adjective 'clean, pure', so 'that I may be found pure bread', with no 'of Christ'. The Nicene Fathers English renders it 'the bread of the world', taking mundus as the noun. The Latin of Irenaeus, as Lightfoot reports it, also has 'of Christ' in the first half ('wheat of Christ') where the Greek has 'of God'.
